node.title: Application of junction diode -diode as a rectifier.

questions.stem: How many diodes does a bridge rectifier use?
options: Two diodes, connected to the two ends of the secondary so that one conducts in each half-cycle
One diode, connected in series so that it conducts in only one half-cycle of the input
Three diodes, connected so that one conducts in the first half-cycle and two in the next
Four diodes, connected so that two of them conduct in each half-cycle
questions.explanation: A bridge rectifier arranges four diodes in a loop. In one half-cycle one pair conducts and in the other half-cycle the second pair conducts, so the current through the load always has the same direction and the circuit does not need a centre-tapped transformer.

optionRationale.1: Two diodes with a centre tap are used in the centre-tap rectifier.
optionRationale.2: A single diode is a half-wave rectifier.
optionRationale.3: The diodes conduct in pairs, with no arrangement of one and two.

questions.objective: Recall the structure of a bridge rectifier

questions.stem: The secondary of a transformer gives $12\,\text{V}$ (rms) to a half-wave rectifier with an ideal diode. What is the peak value of the output voltage?
questions.explanation: The peak value of a sinusoid is $\sqrt2$ times its rms value, so $V_m = 12\times1.414 = 17\,\text{V}$. An ideal diode passes the positive half-cycles without loss, so the output peak equals the input peak.

optionRationale.1: Divides by $\sqrt2$ instead of multiplying, giving a value below the rms value.
optionRationale.3: Takes the rms value as the peak, forgetting the factor $\sqrt2$.
optionRationale.4: Doubles the rms value, which is not the factor for a sine wave.

questions.objective: Convert an rms value to a peak value

questions.stem: A full-wave rectifier is connected to $60\,\text{Hz}$ mains. What is the frequency of the ripple in its output?
questions.explanation: A full-wave rectifier turns each half-cycle of the input into an output pulse, so there are two pulses in every input cycle, and the output ripple frequency is twice the input frequency: $2\times60 = 120\,\text{Hz}$.

optionRationale.2: This is the ripple frequency of a half-wave rectifier, equal to the input frequency.
optionRationale.3: Halves the input frequency instead of doubling it.
optionRationale.4: Doubles twice, giving four times the input frequency.

questions.objective: Find the ripple frequency of a full-wave rectifier

questions.stem: A sinusoidal input of peak value $20\,\text{V}$ is applied to an ideal half-wave rectifier. What is the rms value of the output across the load?
questions.explanation: Squaring the output, the conducting half-cycle contributes $V_m^{2}\sin^{2}\omega t$ and the other half zero. The mean square is therefore $V_m^{2}/4$, so $V_{\text{rms}} = V_m/2 = 10\,\text{V}$. A full sine wave would give $V_m/\sqrt2$.

optionRationale.1: This is the rms value of the complete sine wave, which a half-wave rectifier does not give.
optionRationale.2: This is the average value of the half-wave output, $V_m/\pi$, not the rms value.

questions.objective: Find the rms output of a half-wave rectifier

questions.stem: A bridge rectifier uses silicon diodes, each with a forward drop of $0.7\,\text{V}$. The transformer secondary gives a peak of $12\,\text{V}$. What is the peak voltage across the load?
questions.explanation: In every half-cycle the current passes through two diodes in series, so the voltage lost is $2\times0.7 = 1.4\,\text{V}$. The peak across the load is $12 - 1.4 = 10.6\,\text{V}$. With ideal diodes the full $12\,\text{V}$ peak would appear, so the loss of $1.4\,\text{V}$ matters at low voltages.

optionRationale.1: Subtracts only one diode drop, but two diodes conduct at a time.
optionRationale.2: Neglects the diode drops, which is the ideal-diode result.
optionRationale.3: Subtracts four diode drops, but only two diodes conduct at a time.

questions.objective: Find the load voltage of a bridge rectifier with real diodes

questions.stem: In a centre-tap full-wave rectifier each half of the secondary gives a peak of $20\,\text{V}$. What is the peak inverse voltage that each diode must withstand?
questions.explanation: When one diode conducts, the other is reverse biased and the full secondary voltage, the sum of the two halves, acts across it. The peak inverse voltage is $2V_m = 2\times20 = 40\,\text{V}$.

optionRationale.2: This is the peak of one half of the winding and ignores the voltage of the conducting half.
optionRationale.4: Multiplies the half-winding peak by $\sqrt2$, as if converting to an rms value.

questions.objective: Find the peak inverse voltage in a centre-tap rectifier

questions.stem:
Consider the following statements about the bridge rectifier.
A. It uses four diodes.
B. Two diodes conduct in each half-cycle of the input.
C. The current through the load has the same direction in both half-cycles.
D. It requires a centre-tapped transformer.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below.
questions.explanation: A bridge rectifier has four diodes (A), and in each half-cycle a different pair conducts (B), so the load current always flows the same way (C). The bridge works directly from the full secondary winding and needs no centre tap, so D is false.

optionRationale.1: Includes D, which is false, and leaves out B and C.
optionRationale.3: Leaves out A and includes the false statement D.
optionRationale.4: Includes D, but the centre tap belongs to the two-diode full-wave rectifier.

questions.objective: Evaluate statements about the bridge rectifier

questions.stem: A full-wave rectifier fed from $50\,\text{Hz}$ mains has a $1000\,\mu\text{F}$ filter capacitor and supplies a load current of $20\,\text{mA}$. Treating the capacitor as discharging at constant current between pulses, what is the peak-to-peak ripple voltage?
questions.explanation: Pulses arrive at $100\,\text{Hz}$, so the capacitor discharges for about $\Delta t = 1/100\,\text{s} = 10\,\text{ms}$. The ripple is $\Delta V = I\Delta t/C = (0.020)(0.010)/(1000\times10^{-6}) = 0.20\,\text{V}$. A larger capacitor or a higher pulse frequency makes this ripple smaller.

optionRationale.1: Uses $50\,\text{Hz}$, the ripple frequency of a half-wave rectifier.
optionRationale.2: Halves the correct value, a stray factor of 2.

questions.objective: Estimate the ripple voltage with a filter capacitor

questions.stem: A half-wave rectifier is fed with a sinusoidal peak of $50\,\text{V}$. The load is $1.0\,\text{k}\Omega$ and the diode has a forward resistance of $100\,\Omega$. What is the average load current?
questions.explanation: The peak current is $I_m = V_m/(R_L + r_d) = 50/1100 = 45.5\,\text{mA}$. For a half-wave rectified sine the average current is $I_m/\pi = 14.5\,\text{mA}$. Including the diode resistance lowers the current by about nine per cent compared with the ideal value.

optionRationale.1: Ignores the diode resistance, taking $I_m = V_m/R_L$.
optionRationale.2: This is the peak current and not the average.
optionRationale.4: Uses the full-wave average, $2I_m/\pi$, which does not apply to a half-wave circuit.

questions.objective: Find the average current in a half-wave rectifier

questions.stem:
Assertion (A): The fundamental frequency of the ripple at the output of a half-wave rectifier is equal to the frequency of the input.
Reason (R): In a half-wave rectifier the diode conducts during both half-cycles of the input.
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
questions.explanation: A half-wave rectifier gives one output pulse for every input cycle, so the fundamental ripple frequency equals the input frequency, and A is true. The diode conducts only during one half-cycle, in which it is forward biased, so R is false.

optionRationale.1: Not the answer: R is false, so the pair cannot be true and explaining.
optionRationale.2: Not the answer: R is false, so it is not a true statement that fails to explain A.
optionRationale.4: Not the answer: A is true, since there is one pulse per input cycle.

questions.objective: Relate ripple frequency to the conduction of the diode

questions.stem: Match each part of a rectifier power supply in List-I with its function in List-II.

left: C. A filter capacitor across the load
right: I. Brings the AC voltage to the level required
II. Let the current pass in one direction only
III. Smooths the pulsating output by supplying the load between the peaks
IV. Develops the output voltage from the rectified current

questions.explanation: The transformer lowers the mains voltage to the value the circuit needs (A-I). Diodes conduct only when forward biased and so pass current one way (B-II). The capacitor charges near each peak and discharges slowly through the load, smoothing the output (C-III). The load resistor converts the rectified current into the output voltage (D-IV).

optionRationale.1: Swaps A and B: the diodes rectify and the transformer changes the voltage level.
optionRationale.3: Swaps C and D: the capacitor smooths the output and the resistor develops the output voltage.
optionRationale.4: Swaps A and C: the transformer changes the voltage level and the capacitor smooths the output.

questions.objective: Describe the function of each part of a rectifier circuit

questions.stem: A sinusoidal input of peak $10\,\text{V}$ is applied to a half-wave rectifier with a silicon diode that conducts only when the voltage across it exceeds $0.7\,\text{V}$. For what fraction of each cycle does the diode conduct?
questions.explanation: The diode conducts when $10\sin\omega t > 0.7$, which starts at $\omega t = \sin^{-1}(0.07) = 4.0^{\circ}$ and ends at $180^{\circ} - 4.0^{\circ}$. The conduction angle is $172^{\circ}$ of the $360^{\circ}$ cycle, which is $47.8\,\%$, slightly less than the ideal $50\,\%$.

optionRationale.2: This is the value for an ideal diode, which has no threshold.
optionRationale.3: This is a fraction of the positive half-cycle, not of the whole cycle.
optionRationale.4: Adds the threshold angles instead of subtracting them, giving more than $50\,\%$.

questions.objective: Find the conduction angle of a real diode in a rectifier

questions.stem: In a half-wave rectifier the diode is connected the wrong way round. What does the load voltage look like?
options: Pulses of the same polarity as before, appearing during the positive half-cycles of the input
A steady voltage, because the reversed diode blocks the alternating part of the input
Pulses of the opposite polarity, appearing during the negative half-cycles of the input
No voltage at all, because a reversed diode blocks the current in both half-cycles
questions.explanation: Reversing the diode swaps the half-cycle in which it is forward biased. It now conducts during the negative half-cycles of the input and the load gets pulses of the opposite polarity, while during the positive half-cycles it blocks. The output is still unidirectional, but negative.

optionRationale.1: The diode now conducts in the other half-cycle, so the pulses come in the negative half and have the opposite polarity.
optionRationale.2: A pulsating output is not steady; a steady output needs a filter capacitor.
optionRationale.4: The reversed diode still conducts in one of the half-cycles, so the load sees pulses.

questions.objective: Predict the output of a half-wave rectifier with a reversed diode
